Seminar Title:

Investigating the effects of surface treatment and microstructural modification on the corrosion behavior of stir-cast Al-Cu-Mg based alloys

Seminar Type:

Defence Seminar

Department:

Ceramic Engineering

Speaker Name:

Yogendra Mahton ( Rollno : 516cr1005)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

Seminar Room, CR

Date and Time:

06 Mar 2026 10.30 AM

Contact:

Partha Saha

Abstract:

Aluminum (Al) and its alloys are considered promising materials for lightweight engineering applications, owing to their low density, high strength-to-weight ratio, excellent castability, and desirable mechanical properties. However, their practical utilization is often restricted by inadequate corrosion resistance, particularly in saline environments. To overcome this fundamental limitation, the present work aims to develop a high-strength Al-4.2Cu-1.5Mg-0.56Mn-0.37Si (wt.%) alloy using the stir casting technique. The enhancements in microhardness, tensile, and compressive strength were associated with the development of a refined grain structure containing secondary strengthening phases such as Al2Cu(θ), Al2CuMg(S), and Al5Si(CuMg), which hinder dislocation movement. Nevertheless, the alloy exhibited poor corrosion resistance in saline environments due to the presence of intermetallic phases that formed micro-galvanic couples with the α-Al matrix, thereby promoting intergranular and pitting corrosion. Surface engineering approaches, including cerium-based conversion coating (CeCC), organic coating, and electroless plating, were applied individually and in combination to evaluate corrosion behavior and its relationship with the microstructure. The CeCC treatment produced a mixed oxide-hydroxide layer that preferentially deposited on Cu-rich intermetallic phases owing to their higher electrochemical potential, leading to a non-uniform cathodic coating. To overcome the non-uniformity of the coating, a mussel-inspired polydopamine (PDA) coating was investigated, which enhanced surface coverage by adhering uniformly to both grain boundaries and the α-Al matrix via hydrogen bonding with surface hydroxyls and functional groups. This duplex coating provided both anodic and cathodic protection, resulting in a modest improvement in corrosion resistance. However, the polymer coating is soft and lacks long-term durability, electroless (Ni, Ni-P, and Ni-xCu-P (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 gL-1 CuSO4) coatings were extensively investigated to enhance the corrosion resistance of the Al-Cu-Mg alloy. The optimized Ni-0.1Cu-P coating produced an ~4 μm thick, dense, amorphous layer that exhibited superior corrosion resistance relative to both the Ni-P coating and the bare specimen. Further enhancements were attained through suitable pretreatment (zincating) followed by post-deposition annealing at 100°C, 120°C, and 200°C. The specimen annealed at 120°C displayed a dense, ~5 μm amorphous coating featuring enhanced surface finish, and preserved phosphorus content, leading to superior corrosion resistance. The corrosion resistance was further improved by integrating Ni-0.1Cu-P coated specimens with CeCC sealant with varying sealing duration of 15, 30, and 60 min, followed by annealing at 120°C. The Ni-Cu-P/Ce30-HT specimen demonstrated a refined and uniform surface with reduced surface roughness and densely populated CeO2 particles. This hybrid coating provided the best corrosion resistance, with the lowest corrosion current density (Icorr: ~0.09 μA/cm2) and highest polarization resistance (RP: ~405 kΩ·cm2) among all the specimens investigated. In summary, the present work demonstrates the successful fabrication of a high-strength Al-Cu-Mg alloy, and reveals that integrated surface treatment strategies can substantially improve its corrosion resistance in salt-water solution.
